lines.text: Beyond the nuclear family lies the extended family — a wider network of relatives connected by blood or marriage. Grandparents — a grandmother and grandfather — often play a central role, offering wisdom, childcare, and a sense of heritage. Aunts and uncles are the siblings of your parents, and their children are your cousins. These relationships create a web of support that many families rely on. In-laws enter the picture through marriage: a mother-in-law, father-in-law, sister-in-law, and brother-in-law become part of your family when you marry. A niece is the daughter of your sibling, and a nephew is the son. Great-grandparents sit at the top of the family tree, representing the oldest living generation. Family reunions bring these extended relatives together, strengthening bonds across generations. In many cultures, the extended family lives under one roof or in close proximity, sharing resources and responsibilities. Grandchildren bring joy to grandparents and complete the generational cycle. Understanding extended family vocabulary allows you to navigate family trees, describe relationships accurately, and participate in conversations about family heritage and kinship.

lines.text: In English-speaking cultures, in-law relationships can be complex. 'Mother-in-law jokes' are a comedy staple. The relationship between a person and their in-laws varies widely — from very close to deliberately distant. Using first names vs 'Mum/Dad' for in-laws depends on the family.

lines.text: English has precise cousin terminology: 'first cousins' share grandparents, 'second cousins' share great-grandparents. 'Once removed' means one generation apart. These terms are rarely used in daily conversation but appear in legal and genealogy contexts.

lines.text: English has many affectionate names for grandparents: Grandma/Grandpa, Nana/Papa, Granny/Granddad, Nanny/Pop, Gran/Gramps. Each family chooses their own, and the choice often reflects regional or cultural background.
